nameStory: The Giant Atlantic Cockle gets its name from its impressive size - it's one of the largest cockles found along the Atlantic coast. The word 'cockle' comes from the Old French 'coquille' meaning shell, and these heart-shaped clams certainly live up to their giant reputation compared to their smaller cousins.
description: The Giant Atlantic Cockle is a large saltwater clam that lives buried in sandy ocean bottoms. Its thick, heavy shell has two matching halves (called valves) that can grow quite large - up to 5-6 inches across. The shell has a distinctive heart shape when viewed from the side, with prominent ribs radiating out from the hinge like the spokes of a fan. These impressive mollusks are true giants of the cockle world.

idTips.label: Heart-shaped profile
idTips.description: When viewed from the side, the shell forms a distinct heart shape that's much more pronounced than other cockles - you can easily trace the heart outline with your finger

idTips.label: Prominent ribs
idTips.description: About 32-36 raised ribs radiate from the hinge area like bicycle spokes, creating deep grooves you can feel with your fingertip

idTips.label: Massive size
idTips.description: Much larger than typical cockles - adult shells feel surprisingly heavy in your hand and can span the width of your palm

idTips.label: Thick, sturdy shell
idTips.description: The shell walls are notably thick and solid, making a satisfying 'thunk' sound when tapped, unlike the lighter tap of smaller clams

idTips.label: Yellowish-brown color
idTips.description: Fresh shells range from cream to yellowish-brown with darker growth bands, though beach-worn specimens may be bleached white

habitat: Giant Atlantic Cockles live in sandy or muddy bottoms in shallow coastal waters from the low tide zone down to about 100 feet deep. In New England, they're most commonly found south of Cape Cod in warmer waters. Their empty shells occasionally wash up on beaches after storms, particularly on south-facing shores of southern Massachusetts and Rhode Island.

seasonality.spring: Fresh shells may wash ashore after winter storms. This is a good time to find specimens on beaches as wave action increases.
seasonality.summer: Peak beachcombing season for finding shells. Living specimens are active in warmer waters but remain buried in sand.
seasonality.fall: Storm activity may bring more shells to shore. Late fall storms can uncover specimens from deeper waters.
seasonality.winter: Harsh weather can wash shells onto beaches. Living cockles remain buried deeper in sediment during cold months.

funFact: Giant Atlantic Cockles can actually jump! When threatened, they use their powerful muscular foot to propel themselves several inches off the seafloor - imagine a clam the size of your fist suddenly hopping away like a startled frog underwater.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with other large clams, but the distinctive heart shape when viewed from the side is the dead giveaway - no other large clam in New England waters has such a pronounced heart profile. Remember: 'Heart-shaped cockle, giant-sized trouble for predators!'
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called the 'Atlantic' Giant Cockle, these clams prefer warmer waters and are much more common south of New England. Finding one in New England waters or beaches is actually quite special - they're at the very northern edge of their range here.
compareHints: This is the only giant cockle species in New England waters, making identification straightforward. Compared to other cockles in the true cockle family, it's dramatically larger and has a much more pronounced heart shape. While common cockles might fit in a tablespoon, Giant Atlantic Cockles could fill a soup bowl.
